Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Vignette:
Thomas sat in his truck long after he should have parked, his hands resting lightly on the steering wheel, waiting for the tightness in his chest to ease. The assault had occurred eleven months earlier, outside a convenience store off the main road. A stranger had stepped from the shadows, demanded his wallet, and when Thomas hesitated, the man produced a heavy tire iron. Thomas had backed into a narrow service alley, shoulders pressing against cold brick, hands raised in a defensive arc, knees bent to absorb a blow that never landed but felt inevitable. The attacker’s breathing was ragged, the metal glinting under the streetlamp, before he turned and vanished into the night. Thomas had never been able to reconstruct the sequence when asked to write an incident report or speak to his wife. When the district counselor asked him to draft a formal statement, Thomas sat at his desk for twenty minutes, pen hovering over the paper, until he set it down and admitted he couldn’t piece it together. The deliberate attempt to remember only left him staring at a blank space, his mind refusing to hold the pieces. Yet when the memory surfaced unbidden, it arrived as a clear film, playing over and over in his mind. Each time it surfaced, Thomas felt his own body settle into the exact posture he had held in the alley: shoulders hunched forward, elbows tucked, weight braced on the balls of his feet, as if the threat were still pressing against his back. The school occupied much of his days, and the building became a constant landscape of assessment. Thomas walked through the main doors each morning and immediately tracked the fire exit, the side corridor, the stairwell leading to the parking garage. His attention drifted to anything that could be wielded: the heavy brass paper cutter in the copy room, the fire extinguisher mounted at the end of the administrative wing, the metal legs of the library shelving units. When a substitute dropped a stack of standardized tests in the hallway the previous Tuesday, Thomas’s spine snapped straight, his breath caught, and his shoulders tensed as if a blow were imminent. He did not tell himself he was hyperalert; he simply felt the atmosphere shift, and his body moved to brace. Over the months, these experiences settled into a quiet architecture of daily life. Thomas began taking the faculty service entrance to avoid the crowded lunchroom. He stopped lingering after parent conferences. His wife noticed how he flinched when he thought he heard a garage door close, how he would pause mid-sentence and check the room’s perimeter before continuing. The habit of checking door placements meant he often arrived to morning staff meetings late, fumbling with his keys as he mapped the room. His authority, once built on easy movement and open doors, now felt constrained by an invisible grid of escape routes. His wife, Elena, watched him untangle his hands after the morning drill, her own quiet routine unfolding alongside his without either of them naming the weight he carried. At fifty-two, married, and holding a career he had spent two decades building, Thomas finally sought help after a morning fire drill triggered a full-body freeze in the administrative wing. He came to the clinic because the watching, the replay, the sudden jolts of his nervous system were bleeding into his marriage and his work. He didn’t want to live like a man perpetually bracing for an ambush, and he hoped, quietly, to find a way to step through a doorway without first measuring the distance to the exit.
